narrative.text: The table of contents of the 2020 WHO guidelines on TB preventive treatment, listing chapters and online annexes.

Acknowledges the WHO Global TB Programme staff who coordinated the guidelines and lists the members of the Guideline Development Group and other contributors. It also thanks the Guideline Review Committee and names USAID and the Russian Federation as funders of the 2019–2020 update. The names and affiliations come from many countries.
A list of abbreviations and acronyms used in the TB preventive treatment guidelines, including regimen codes such as 3HP and 1HP.

Defines terms used in the TB preventive treatment guidelines, such as age groups, contact investigation, household contact and high TB transmission setting. It also defines TB disease as distinct from TB infection and underweight in adults and children.

The executive summary of the 2020 guidelines, defining latent TB infection, noting that about a quarter of the world's population is infected, and placing preventive treatment within the End TB Strategy. It describes the intended users and the aims of the update. It lists the main changes, including recommendations reworded to apply regardless of TB burden, adding 1-month rifapentine plus isoniazid and 4-month rifampicin as options in all settings, and simplified regimen durations. It also notes that a single algorithm replaces four earlier ones and that references and research gaps were updated.

Gives background on latent TB infection, noting that 5–10% of those infected develop active disease, usually within five years, and that immune status is the main risk factor. It recalls the 2018 UN high-level meeting commitment to provide preventive treatment to 30 million people by 2022 and places it within the End TB Strategy.

Explains the rationale for the guidelines, which weigh risk of progression, TB burden, feasibility and public health impact and are meant to be adapted nationally. It notes low global coverage and that new evidence since the 2018 consolidated guidelines required revisiting some recommendations.

Describes the scope of the update, which addressed three PICO questions on 4-month rifampicin, 1-month rifapentine plus isoniazid, and isoniazid safety in pregnant and postpartum women. It notes that wording was clarified and that the earlier distinction between high- and low-incidence settings was reconsidered, with evidence judged using GRADE evidence-to-decision criteria.

Identifies the target audience as national TB, HIV and maternal and child health programmes and other policy-makers, staff of agencies such as prison and immigration services, and clinicians in public and private sectors.

The main recommendations chapter of the 2020 TB preventive treatment guidelines, which begins by explaining why preventive treatment should target groups at highest risk of progression. It gives recommendations and supporting evidence for adults, adolescents, infants and children living with HIV, citing trial data on reduced TB risk and added benefit alongside antiretroviral therapy. The chapter goes on to cover other risk groups, testing and treatment options across a long, cut section. It ends with preventive treatment for contacts of people with multidrug-resistant TB, advising individualized fluoroquinolone-based regimens and written informed consent given very low-certainty evidence.

Describes monitoring and evaluation of programmatic TB preventive treatment, including core indicators, national recording and reporting systems and involving the private sector. It covers adverse drug reactions, monthly follow-up, warning symptoms of hepatotoxicity and when baseline liver testing is advised. It ends with clinical follow-up of contacts exposed to multidrug-resistant TB for at least two years and attention to drug interactions.

Sets out research gaps in TB preventive treatment, including risk of progression in groups such as people with diabetes or who smoke, and better algorithms for ruling out active TB. It calls for improved diagnostic tests for infection and shorter, better-tolerated regimens, with more data on rifapentine in young children and pregnancy. It also lists needs on implementation, contact tracing strategies and monitoring tools.
The reference list for the TB preventive treatment guidelines, with over 100 citations to journal studies and WHO and UN documents on TB infection, treatment and policy.

A supplementary table comparing WHO's 2018 recommendations on tuberculosis preventive treatment with those in the current update, section by section. A note explains that two LTBI testing recommendations became implementation remarks and that four regimen recommendations were merged into one. Each row pairs the old and new wording for groups such as people living with HIV, infants and children, and household contacts, marking whether changes were language edits or substantive. It closes with the recommendation on 36 months of isoniazid in high-transmission settings and WHO Global TB Programme contact details.
The title, copyright, licence and cataloguing pages of the WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, Module 1: prevention, on TB preventive treatment (2020), with ISBNs.
